name: KurrentDB
license: Kurrent License v1 (source available; no offering it as a hosted service, some features need a license key) since 25.0 in March 2025; Event Store License v2 for 24.10; 3-clause BSD up to 24.6

status.note: Called EventStoreDB until version 25.0 on 13 March 2025; the company, Event Store, renamed itself Kurrent in December 2024.

summary: A database built for event sourcing, formerly EventStoreDB: it appends immutable events to one ordered log, groups them into per-entity streams, and pushes them to subscribers.
intro: KurrentDB keeps every event in a single append-only log, stored as a series of data files (chunks, 256 MB by default) in the order the events were written. Each event also belongs to a stream, named by the application and usually one per entity, such as `order-123`, and an append writes to the log and the stream at once. Reading a stream returns just that entity’s events, which the application replays to rebuild its state. Every append can name the state the writer expects the stream to be in (`NO_STREAM`, `EXISTS` or an exact version), and fails if another writer got there first: optimistic concurrency, per stream, without locks. Retrying an append with the same event IDs doesn’t write duplicates, and one append can cover several streams atomically. Events are never edited; you can only truncate a stream, cap it by age or count, or delete it.

Events flow out through subscriptions. A catch-up subscription reads from a position the client keeps, then follows new events live, in order. A persistent subscription keeps its position on the server and spreads events over a consumer group of competing consumers, with at-least-once delivery, retries and a parked-message stream for events that keep failing. Projections, written in JavaScript and run inside the server, react to JSON events and emit or link them into new streams. Secondary indexes on category and event type (25.1), user-defined indexes (26.0) and SQL queries over the indexed log (through Arrow Flight SQL since 26.1, run by an embedded DuckDB engine) now cover many queries that used to need a projection.

A cluster is shared-nothing: every node holds a full copy, writes go to the elected leader, and a write is acknowledged once a majority of nodes has it, so tolerating n failed nodes takes 2n + 1. Nodes find each other by gossip and elect the leader with a Paxos-based algorithm; 26.2 adds an optional Raft-based Kontrol Plane that appoints the leader instead. The server is written in C# and runs self-hosted on Linux, Windows, macOS or Docker, or managed as Kurrent Cloud on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud, with official gRPC clients for Python, Java, .NET, Node.js, Go and Rust.
strengths: The event-sourcing primitives are built in: per-entity streams, an expected-version check on every append, idempotent retries by event ID and atomic multi-stream appends
One log feeds many readers: in-order catch-up subscriptions for read models, and persistent subscriptions with server-side checkpoints, consumer groups and retries for work queues
Queries over the history without a second database: projections, secondary and user-defined indexes, and SQL through Arrow Flight SQL

From 26.2 a single node runs in production with no license key, including backup and point-in-time recovery, connectors (Kafka, RabbitMQ, MongoDB, Elasticsearch, Pulsar, PostgreSQL), OAuth, LDAP and OpenTelemetry export
limits: Source available, not open source: the Kurrent License v1 forbids offering it to others as a hosted or managed service, and forbids working around its license-key checks

From 26.2 every multi-node deployment needs an Enterprise license key on all nodes, even for development and test: high-availability clusters, read-only replicas and so archiving, whose archiver node is a replica
Only the leader takes writes, and the cluster size is fixed in configuration: adding a node means changing `ClusterSize` on every node first

You can’t delete one event from the middle of a stream; deleted and expired events only free space when a scavenge runs, and a deleted stream keeps one event as a marker. Projections only read JSON events

story: Event sourcing stores every change as a fact instead of overwriting the current state, which turns the database into a kind of time machine: you can write a new report today and run it as if it were a month ago. Event Store was built for exactly that. It was first released in September 2012, as open source under a 3-clause BSD license, with Greg Young, the consultant who coined the term CQRS, as lead architect. Greg Young’s interest in “temporal correlation queries”, questions that link things that happened at different times, shaped its JavaScript query language over streams, which became projections.

For twelve years the database stayed BSD-licensed, beside a separate commercial edition. In September 2024 Event Store announced that EventStoreDB 24.10 would ship as one build for everyone under the Event Store License v2, based on the Elastic License v2, with enterprise features unlocked by a license key and all source still public. In December 2024 the company renamed itself Kurrent and raised $12 million in a round led by Crane Venture Partners; CEO Kirk Dunn said the name describes data flowing like electrical current through a company, and the announcement described Kurrent as founded in 2019 by Greg Young and based in San Francisco. KurrentDB 25.0, on 13 March 2025, was the first release under the new name and the new Kurrent License v1.

Two years after introducing the key, Kurrent moved the line. Its features had been chosen as signs of scale, but connectors, authentication and observability turned out to be what small teams needed too, so few users had a reason to buy. From 26.2 nearly every licensed feature is free on a single node, and what needs a license is running more than one node, which Kurrent calls the most reliable sign that a database runs something commercially important.

choices.choice: One global log, with streams as the unit you read and lock
choices.why: Every event is appended to the log and to its stream at the same time. Fine-grained streams per entity make reads fast and give each entity its own optimistic concurrency check, while the global log keeps one order for subscribers that want everything.

Catch-up subscriptions keep their position in the client and process events in order; persistent subscriptions keep it on the server so a group of consumers can share the work, at the price of events arriving out of order within a window.

choices.choice: Queries written in JavaScript, running inside the database
choices.why: Temporal correlation queries, such as finding patients put on one treatment within three weeks of a diagnosis, run continuously over the events, and their output is just another stream. JavaScript meant a web browser could be used to write and debug them.

choices.choice: A license key instead of separate builds
choices.why: Since 24.10 everyone downloads the same package and the source stays readable, while a key turns on the paid features, which Kurrent says funds continued development of the product.
